---
title: "Visits with Unobserved States"
---

```{r vignette-options, include = FALSE}
source("../_setup.R", local = TRUE)
```

In most trials some daily states are never recorded: an assessment is
skipped, a patient at home cannot be reached, or a form is lost. The patient
is then seen again later, or dies later, and the state on the days in
between is unknown. This article shows how to give such data to `mostm()` so
that every recorded state is used, why leaving out the incomplete visits
biases the results, and what assumption the analysis rests on.

The article covers

1. why dropping the visits around a missing state overestimates death;
2. how to lay out the data, with `NA` for an unknown state and
   `Ocens(lower, upper)` for a state that is partly known;
3. fitting with `engine = "orm"` and comparing the results with those from
   the complete data and from dropping the incomplete visits;
4. how the calculation works and when it is valid;
5. Bayesian fits with `engine = "blrm"`; and
6. restrictions and the error messages you may meet.

## Why dropping incomplete visits is biased

A transition model describes each visit's state given the state at the
visit before. A row of the model data is therefore usable on its own only
when both its state and its previous state are known. A missing state on one
day removes two transitions: the one into that day and the one out of it.

Deaths are usually recorded even when other assessments are missed, for
example from hospital records or a death registry. Suppose a quarter of the
states of living patients are missing, at random. A transition between two
living states is kept only if both of its states were recorded, which
happens for about 0.75 × 0.75 = 56% of them. A transition into death is kept
whenever the visit before it was recorded, which happens for 75% of them.
Among the rows that are kept, deaths are therefore over-represented by a
factor of about 0.75 / 0.56 = 1.33, and a model fitted to those rows
overestimates the risk of death.

`mostm()` avoids this by keeping every visit. For a patient seen in state 5
on day 4, not seen on days 5 and 6, and dead on day 7, the model adds up the
probabilities of every sequence of states the patient can have been in on
days 5 and 6 and uses the resulting probability of moving from state 5 on
day 4 to death on day 7. Nothing that was recorded is thrown away, and
nothing that was not recorded is made up.

## Example data with missed visits

We simulate 1,000 patients over 28 days with `sim_markov("actt2")`, which
uses the eight-state NIAID scale described in
[the proportional-odds article](full-po-sops.html): states 1 and 2 are
outside hospital, 3 to 7 in hospital with increasing need for respiratory
support, and 8 is death. `prepare_markov_data()` removes the rows after
death. These are the complete data, which a real trial would not have; we
keep them to see how close each analysis comes to them.

```{r setup}
library(mostr)

N_PATIENTS <- 1000
FOLLOW_UP <- 28
SEED <- 20261115
ABSORB <- "8"

complete <- sim_markov(
  "actt2",
  n_patients = N_PATIENTS,
  follow_up_time = FOLLOW_UP,
  treatment_effect = log(0.8),
  seed = SEED
)
complete <- prepare_markov_data(complete, absorbing_state = as.integer(ABSORB))
complete <- complete[order(complete$id, complete$time), ]
```

Next we remove states the way a trial might lose them. Patients at home are
harder to reach than patients in hospital: if the last state recorded for a
patient was 1 or 2 (outside hospital), the next day's state is missing with
probability 0.4, otherwise with probability 0.1. Deaths are always
recorded. Because whether a state is missing depends only on states that
were recorded, the states are *missing at random*, the assumption the
method needs (see below).

On the row after each missed visit the previous state is unknown as well, so
`hide_states()` sets `yprev` to `NA` there too.

```{r hide-states}
hide_states <- function(data, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  data <- data[order(data$id, data$time), ]
  y <- as.integer(as.character(data$y))
  missed <- logical(nrow(data))
  for (rows in split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$id)) {
    # The state before day 1 is the baseline state, which is always known.
    last_recorded <- as.integer(as.character(data$yprev[rows[1]]))
    for (row in rows) {
      p_missed <- if (last_recorded <= 2) 0.4 else 0.1
      if (y[row] != 8 && stats::runif(1) < p_missed) {
        missed[row] <- TRUE
      } else {
        last_recorded <- y[row]
      }
    }
  }
  same_patient <- c(FALSE, data$id[-1] == data$id[-nrow(data)])
  after_missed <- c(FALSE, missed[-nrow(data)]) & same_patient
  data$y[missed] <- NA
  data$yprev[after_missed] <- NA
  data
}

observed <- hide_states(complete, seed = 1)
mean(is.na(observed$y[complete$y != ABSORB]))
```

About a quarter of the states of living patients are now missing. Here are
the first 12 days of one patient, with the complete state next to what was
recorded:

```{r one-patient}
# The first patient with a missed visit in the first week.
patient <- observed$id[which(is.na(observed$y) & observed$time <= 7)[1]]
rows <- complete$id == patient & complete$time <= 12
data.frame(
  time = complete$time[rows],
  y_complete = complete$y[rows],
  y = observed$y[rows],
  yprev = observed$yprev[rows]
)
```

The data keep one row for every visit, in time order. Where the state was
not recorded, `y` is `NA`, and on the following row `yprev` is `NA` as well.
Do not carry the last recorded state forward into `yprev`: the model works
out which states the patient can have been in, and a filled-in value would
claim a state that was never seen. `mostm()` checks this and stops if
`yprev` is filled in after a missing state (see the last section).

What a missing state means depends on where it is:

- **Between two recorded visits**, it is one of the states that are not
  absorbing (here 1 to 7). A patient who is seen alive later, or whose death
  is recorded later on its own visit, was alive in between.
- **After the patient's last recorded state**, it says nothing, not even
  whether the patient was alive: the patient may have been lost to
  follow-up. These rows do not enter the fit, so keeping them gives the same
  fit as removing them. If you know that the patient was alive, say so with
  `Ocens()`, as shown below.

## Fit and compare

We fit the same model three times: to the complete data, to the observed
data with the default `missing_states = "average"`, which adds up over the
unknown states, and to the observed data with `missing_states = "drop"`,
which leaves out every row with a missing state or previous state.

```{r fits}
formula <- y ~ yprev + time + tx

fit_complete <- mostm(formula, data = complete, id_var = "id", absorb = ABSORB)
fit_average <- mostm(formula, data = observed, id_var = "id", absorb = ABSORB)
fit_drop <- mostm(
  formula,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorb = ABSORB,
  missing_states = "drop"
)
```

`missing_states = "average"` is the default for `engine = "orm"` and
`engine = "blrm"`, so `fit_average` needs no extra argument. Each fit takes
about a second here.

The function below estimates the state occupancy probabilities (SOPs) in
each arm with `avg_sops()`, adds 95% confidence intervals with
`inferences(method = "delta")`, which calculates them from formulas without
random draws, and keeps the probability of death and of state 1 (at home,
without limitations) on day 28.

```{r compare}
day_28 <- function(fit, analysis) {
  sops <- avg_sops(fit, variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)), times = 1:FOLLOW_UP) |>
    inferences(method = "delta")
  sops <- as.data.frame(sops)
  sops <- sops[sops$time == FOLLOW_UP & sops$state %in% c("1", ABSORB), ]
  data.frame(
    analysis = analysis,
    state = sops$state,
    tx = sops$tx,
    estimate = round(sops$estimate, 3),
    conf.low = round(sops$conf.low, 3),
    conf.high = round(sops$conf.high, 3)
  )
}

comparison <- rbind(
  day_28(fit_complete, "complete data"),
  day_28(fit_average, "average (default)"),
  day_28(fit_drop, "drop")
)
comparison[order(comparison$state, comparison$tx), ]
```

```{r death-difference, include = FALSE}
death <- function(analysis, arm) {
  comparison$estimate[comparison$analysis == analysis &
    comparison$state == ABSORB & comparison$tx == arm]
}
excess <- function(arm) {
  round(1000 * (death("drop", arm) - death("complete data", arm)))
}
```

With the default, the estimates are within 0.003 of those from the complete
data, and the intervals are only slightly wider, because a quarter of the
states are missing. Dropping the incomplete rows overestimates the
probability of death on day 28 in both arms, by `r excess(0)` per 1,000
patients in the control arm and `r excess(1)` per 1,000 in the treated arm,
as the arithmetic at the start of this article suggests. It changes the
probability of state 1 as well, by up to 0.011 here.

This is one simulated trial. In a simulation of 500 trials with 400
patients each, followed for 28 days, with about a quarter of the states of
living patients missing and deaths always recorded, dropping the incomplete
rows overestimated the day-28 probability of death in the control arm by on
average 17.5 per 1,000 patients when states were missing completely at
random, and by 34.9 per 1,000 when they were missing at random, with
sicker patients missing more often (the true probability was about 71 per
1,000). The default overestimated it by 0.4 and 2.2 per 1,000; the
remaining bias comes from the visits after each patient's last recorded
state, which the next section removes.

## Partly known states with `Ocens()`

Often more is known about a visit than nothing. Give the possible states of
each visit as a range with the response `Ocens(lower, upper)`, where `lower`
and `upper` are columns of the data holding the lowest and the highest state
the patient can have been in:

- an observed state has `lower` equal to `upper`;
- `NA` in both means that nothing is known, as for `y = NA` above;
- `-Inf` and `Inf` stand for the lowest and the highest state.

`mostm()` reads the ranges itself, so you do not need to attach rms to use
`Ocens()`. Two kinds of partial knowledge are common.

**Known to be alive.** In this simulation every death is recorded, so a
patient whose death is not recorded was alive at every visit, also after
the last recorded state. Marking those visits as alive, states 1 to 7,
tells the model that only patients who survive have such visits. Without
it the model overestimates death slightly, as the simulation above showed.
Only mark a visit as alive if you know it: treating patients who were lost
to follow-up as alive makes the model underestimate death, which is the
larger error.

**Known to be in hospital.** Suppose hospital records show whether a patient
was in hospital on a day without an assessment. Then a missed day in
hospital has the range 3 to 7, and a missed day at home 1 to 2. In this
simulation we take that information from the complete data.

```{r ranges}
y_observed <- as.integer(as.character(observed$y))
y_true <- as.integer(as.character(complete$y))
observed$lower <- y_observed
observed$upper <- y_observed

# Visits without a recorded state after the patient's last recorded state.
recorded_later <- ave(
  !is.na(y_observed),
  observed$id,
  FUN = function(recorded) rev(cumsum(rev(recorded))) > 0
)
after_last <- is.na(y_observed) & !recorded_later
observed$lower[after_last] <- 1
observed$upper[after_last] <- 7

# Missed visits between recorded ones: in hospital (3 to 7) or at home (1 to 2).
between <- is.na(y_observed) & recorded_later
in_hospital <- y_true >= 3
observed$lower[between] <- ifelse(in_hospital[between], 3, 1)
observed$upper[between] <- ifelse(in_hospital[between], 7, 2)

observed[observed$id == patient & observed$time <= 12,
         c("time", "y", "yprev", "lower", "upper")]
```

The previous state stays `NA` after every visit whose state is not known
exactly, a range included. The fit uses the same formula with
`Ocens(lower, upper)` as the response:

```{r fit-ranges}
fit_ranges <- mostm(
  Ocens(lower, upper) ~ yprev + time + tx,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorb = ABSORB
)

comparison <- rbind(comparison, day_28(fit_ranges, "Ocens() ranges"))
comparison[order(comparison$state, comparison$tx), ]
```

In this trial the ranges change the estimates and intervals by at most
0.002, because the default already used every recorded state. In the
simulation of
500 trials, marking the visits after the last recorded state as alive
reduced the remaining overestimate of death on day 28 from 0.4 to 0.03 per
1,000 (missing completely at random) and from 2.2 to 0.04 per 1,000
(missing at random).

## How the calculation works

For each visit the model gives the probability of each state given the
state at the visit before, the time and the other predictors. Write
$p_t(j, k)$ for the probability that a patient in state $j$ at visit
$t - 1$ is in state $k$ at visit $t$. Take a patient whose state is known
to be $a$ at visit $u$ and $b$ at a later visit $v$, with unrecorded visits
in between, and let $R_t$ be the set of states the patient can have been in
at visit $t$: the states that are not absorbing, or the range given with
`Ocens()`. The probability of this part of the patient's history is

$$
P(Y_v = b \mid Y_u = a) =
\sum_{s_{u+1} \in R_{u+1}} \cdots \sum_{s_{v-1} \in R_{v-1}}
\; \prod_{t = u + 1}^{v} p_t(s_{t-1}, s_t),
\qquad s_u = a,\; s_v = b,
$$

where $Y_t$ is the patient's state at visit $t$ and $s_{u+1}, \ldots,
s_{v-1}$ run over the states the patient can have been in at the unrecorded
visits. Each term of the sum is one possible sequence of states on those
days, and its probability is the product of the probabilities of the
transitions along it. When the state at visit $v$ is itself a range, the
probability is added up over the states $b$ in that range too.

The number of sequences grows quickly with the length of a gap: a gap of 5
days with 7 possible states has $7^5 = 16{,}807$ of them. So mostr does not
list them. It works through the gap one visit at a time instead: starting
from state $a$ at visit $u$, it calculates the probability of being in each
state of $R_{u+1}$ at the next visit, from these and $p_{u+2}$ the
probabilities of each state of $R_{u+2}$, and so on, until visit $v$. This
is the same visit-by-visit calculation that `avg_sops()` uses for state
occupancy probabilities.

Visits whose state and previous state are both recorded contribute
$p_t(j, k)$ as in an ordinary fit. `engine = "orm"` finds the coefficients
that maximise the product of all these probabilities (the likelihood);
`engine = "blrm"` samples from the posterior distribution it gives.
Standard errors, `inferences()` with every method, and the prediction and
plotting functions work as for a fit to complete data.

## When the method is valid

The calculation is valid when states are **missing at random**: whether a
state is recorded may depend on the predictors and on the patient's
recorded states, before or after the missed visit, but not on the
unrecorded state itself. The example above is missing at random, because
the chance of a missed assessment depends on the last recorded state.

If instead patients are less likely to be assessed on the very days they
are sicker, the missingness depends on the unobserved state, and no method
that uses only the recorded states is free of bias. In the simulation of
500 trials with such missingness, the default overestimated the probability
of being in state 1 on day 28 by about 6 per 1,000 patients, while dropping
the incomplete rows overestimated it by 50 to 115 per 1,000.

Dropping the incomplete rows is biased even when states are missing at
random, as soon as some states, such as death, are recorded more reliably
than others.

## Bayesian fits with `engine = "blrm"`

`engine = "blrm"` uses the same likelihood. rmsb's own Stan programs take
one row per transition and cannot add up over unrecorded states, so mostr
samples with a Stan program of its own. The first fit with unrecorded
states compiles that program, which takes a minute or more and needs a C++
toolchain and the rstan package (or cmdstanr, with `backend = "cmdstan"`).
The compiled program is kept in the directory
`tools::R_user_dir("mostr", "cache")` and reused in later sessions; set
`options(mostr.stan_cache = )` to another directory, or to `FALSE` to keep
it for the current session only.

The chunk below is not run when this article is built.

```{r blrm, eval = FALSE}
# Run the four chains in parallel.
options(mc.cores = 4)

fit_bayes <- mostm(
  Ocens(lower, upper) ~ yprev + time + tx,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorb = ABSORB,
  engine = "blrm",
  iter = 2000,
  chains = 4,
  sampling.args = list(seed = 2026)
)

avg_sops(fit_bayes, variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)), times = 1:FOLLOW_UP)
```

`sampling.args = list(seed = 2026)` makes the posterior draws reproducible;
a `seed` given directly to `mostm()` would not. Without `options(mc.cores)`,
or `cores` in `sampling.args`, the chains run one after another. With data
of this size, sampling takes a few minutes on four cores. The results carry posterior
intervals, so no `inferences()` step is needed; see
[the Bayesian article](bayesian-rmsb-sops.html).

## Restrictions and error messages

**The previous state must be `NA` exactly after a visit that is not known
exactly.** Filling it in, for example with the last recorded state, is an
error:

```{r filled-in, error = TRUE}
carried_forward <- observed
# The first row after a missed visit, given a previous state.
first_after <- which(is.na(carried_forward$yprev))[1]
carried_forward$yprev[first_after] <- "4"
mostm(formula, data = carried_forward, id_var = "id", absorb = ABSORB)
```

The reverse, a missing `yprev` on a row whose previous row has a recorded
state, is an error too. It usually means that the rows of a missed visit
were deleted instead of kept with `y = NA`: add a row for every visit.

**Every state must be observed exactly at least once**, at a visit after the
patient's first known state; a range given with `Ocens()` does not count.
When the previous state is a factor, as here, every state that a missed
visit can follow must also be the last recorded state before at least one
such visit. Merge rarely observed states if `mostm()` reports that a state
is never observed or never a previous state.

**Every visit needs all predictors**, also when its state is missing,
because the model predicts the transitions into and out of it.

**The missing states between two recorded visits must be next to each other
in the order of the states.** With two absorbing states at either end of the
scale, such as discharge home (1) and death (8), the states a missed visit
can be in are 2 to 7; with an absorbing state in the middle, give the
possible states of each missed visit with `Ocens()`.

**Not available together with unrecorded states**: second-order models
(`p2_var`), penalties and links other than the logit for `engine = "orm"`,
partial proportional odds (`ppo`), random effects (`cluster()`) and
`iprior` for `engine = "blrm"`, and row weights that differ within a run of
missed visits (one weight per patient is fine). For these, the only option
is `missing_states = "drop"`, with the bias described above.

**`engine = "vglm"` can only drop the incomplete rows**, and you must ask for
it:

```{r vglm, error = TRUE}
mostm(ordered(y) ~ yprev + time + tx, data = observed, id_var = "id",
      absorb = ABSORB, engine = "vglm")
```

Add `missing_states = "drop"` to accept the bias, or use `engine = "orm"`.
For more on the arguments, see "Unobserved states" in `?mostm`.
